summary: Defines how NSIS QoS signaling can work across IP tunnels, where encapsulation hides the original header fields. It maps end-to-end QoS sessions to sessions inside the tunnel. It is an Experimental protocol.

eli5.summary: If a package goes through a sealed tube, the tube workers can't read the label, so this gives them a copy of the label.

questions: how does qos work in tunnels
subtitle: How to keep QoS reservations working when data packets are tunneled

tldr.problem: When IP packets are tunneled, the original packet headers are hidden inside the tunnel, so NSIS QoS signaling cannot find or classify the data flows inside the tunnel.
tldr.mechanism: Tunnel entry and exit points map end-to-end QoS reservation requests to QoS sessions within the tunnel using tunnel-specific header fields (Flow IDs) instead of the original packet headers.
tldr.outcome: End-to-end QoS signaling can extend into tunnel segments, preventing tunnels from becoming the weakest link in the path.

facts.label: Tunneling protocols supported
facts.value: GRE, IPsec, IPv6, IPv4-in-IPv4, MINENC, and variants

facts.label: Tunnel modes
facts.value: Preconfigured QoS sessions or dynamically created

facts.label: Flow ID variant for IPsec
facts.value: Tunnel endpoints plus Security Parameter Index (SPI)

today: RFC 5979 is an Experimental protocol that defines how to extend NSIS QoS signaling into IP tunnel segments. It has not been updated or obsoleted.

sections.title: The QoS Problem in Tunnels
sections.content:
IP tunneling carries complete packets inside other IP packets, protecting them as they cross networks with different characteristics. However, NSIS Quality of Service (QoS) signaling requires access to the original packet headers to identify flows and apply QoS treatment. Inside a tunnel, the original headers are encapsulated and invisible, so intermediate tunnel nodes cannot process NSIS signaling messages or classify data packets.

This creates a critical gap: end-to-end QoS reservations fail within the tunnel segment, making the tunnel the bottleneck regardless of QoS reservation elsewhere on the path.
sections.eli5: QoS signaling is like giving instructions to routers about which packages need to go fast. But inside a tunnel, those instructions are sealed in a box and the tunnel workers cannot read them.

sections.title: Tunnel-Aware NSIS Endpoints
sections.content:
The solution requires both tunnel entry-point and exit-point nodes to be NSIS-tunnel-aware: they understand both NSIS signaling and tunnel mechanics. When an end-to-end QoS session request arrives at the tunnel entry-point, it maps the request to a tunnel QoS session using a tunnel Flow ID. This Flow ID is computed from tunnel header fields visible to all tunnel nodes (such as the tunnel's source and destination IP addresses, or Security Parameter Indexes in IPsec).

The tunnel exit-point applies the same mapping in reverse, maintaining the association between the end-to-end session and the tunnel session. This enables the tunnel intermediate nodes to intercept and process NSIS signaling for flows identified by the tunnel Flow ID.
sections.eli5: The tunnel workers at both ends agree to copy important information from the original package label onto the outside of the box, so every worker in the tunnel can see it and treat packages the right way.

sections.title: Tunnel Flow IDs for Different Protocols
sections.content:
Different IP tunneling protocols expose different header fields. For IPv6 generic tunneling (IPv6GEN), the Flow ID uses tunnel endpoint addresses plus the IPv6 flow label. For IPsec tunnel mode, it uses tunnel endpoint addresses and the Security Parameter Index (SPI). For other tunneling protocols (GRE, GREIPv4, IPv4INIPv4, MINENC, IPv6INIPv4), the tunnel entry-point inserts an additional UDP header between the tunnel header and the original packet; the Flow ID then uses tunnel endpoint addresses and a dynamically chosen UDP source port.

Preconfigured tunnel QoS sessions rely on whatever Flow ID definition their configuration mechanism provides (for example, Diffserv Code Point fields in Differentiated Services).
sections.eli5: Different types of boxes have different ways to mark what is inside. The tunnel workers learn which marking system their box uses and read the marks to know how to handle each package.

sections.title: Two Modes of Operation
sections.content:
Tunnels may handle QoS in two ways. In the preconfigured QoS mode, the tunnel already has reserved QoS sessions. The tunnel entry-point simply maps arriving end-to-end requests to existing tunnel sessions based on policy. No new tunnel signaling is needed.

In the dynamically created QoS mode, the tunnel endpoints use NSIS signaling inside the tunnel to establish QoS sessions on demand. This involves coordinating two signaling sequences: one for the end-to-end session (outside the tunnel) and one for the tunnel session (inside the tunnel). The entry-point generates a tunnel RESERVE message matching the end-to-end request and forwards it to the exit-point. Both endpoints record the binding between sessions and use NSIS message binding mechanisms (MSG-ID and BOUND-SESSION-ID objects) to synchronize the two sequences.
sections.eli5: Either the tunnel already has marked lanes for different types of packages (preconfigured), or the tunnel workers create new lanes on demand (dynamic) when a special package arrives that needs them.

sections.title: Security and Capability Discovery
sections.content:
NSIS-tunnel-aware endpoints must know whether the other tunnel endpoint supports this mechanism before attempting to use it. Preconfigured tunnels can establish this through configuration; otherwise, the endpoints use a NODE_CAPABILITY_TUNNEL object in NSIS signaling messages to discover each other's support.

When NSIS signaling is used with IPsec tunnels, a potential covert channel exists: an entity inside the IPsec tunnel could create spurious NSIS signaling flows to communicate with the outside network. This risk applies to any signaling with per-hop processing inside encrypted tunnels; rate-limiting and policy controls are necessary. General NSIS security threats are covered in RFC 4081.
sections.eli5: Before the tunnel workers start using the new system, they need to check that both ends support it. With encrypted tunnels, there is a risk that someone could sneak hidden messages through the signaling, so there are rules to prevent that.
